definition: Calm, carefree and unbothered, often when others think worry is called for.
example: She gave an insouciant shrug when the train was announced as an hour late.
nuance: Insouciant suggests a breezy, lighthearted freedom from worry; nonchalant stresses a cool, composed outward manner.
prompt: A pianist waits backstage a few minutes before her first big recital.
options: Humming softly, the pianist seemed insouciant while the other performers paced the hallway.
The insouciant pianist was so nervous that she nearly fled the building before her turn.
The insouciant pianist sneered at the stage manager and called him a worthless fool.
The pianist had insouciant time to warm up, so she skipped her scales and hoped for the best.
reasons: Staying relaxed and untroubled while others fret captures the breezy calm the word describes.
Overwhelming nerves are the reverse of a lighthearted, unworried attitude.
Open contempt is insolence, a look-alike word; this one means carefree, not rude.
This confuses the word with insufficient; it describes a person's mood, not an amount.

practice.prompt: A hiker realizes the trail map was left in the car several miles behind.
options: He was insouciant that they turn back at once, repeating the demand until everyone agreed.
The insouciant trail climbed steeply over loose rocks and fallen logs toward the ridge.
With an insouciant grin, he said they would simply follow the river and see where it led.
Pale and gasping, he grew insouciant as he pictured being lost in the woods after dark.
reasons: This mistakes the word for insistent; it names a carefree manner, not a firm demand.
A trail has no feelings; the word describes a person's attitude or manner.
Treating a real setback with easygoing cheer shows exactly this kind of unbothered spirit.
Panic and fear are the opposite of a relaxed, worry-free outlook.
